claims: El Niño is a climate pattern marked by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific Ocean.
El Niño typically occurs every 2-7 years.
El Niño often brings wetter, cooler conditions to the Southern US.
El Niño often brings warmer, drier conditions to the North.
El Niño shifts the Pacific jet stream southward.
Enhanced storm activity often occurs in the southern US, Peru, Ecuador, and parts of the Caribbean during El Niño.
Increased precipitation often occurs in the southern US, Peru, Ecuador, and parts of the Caribbean during El Niño.
Drought often strikes Indonesia, Australia, and parts of Africa during El Niño.
Extreme heat often strikes Indonesia, Australia, and parts of Africa during El Niño.
The southern tier of the U.S. experiences wetter and colder conditions during North American winter during El Niño.
Northern U.S. states and Canada tend to be warmer and drier than average during North American winter during El Niño.
El Niño generally increases Pacific hurricane activity.
El Niño decreases nutrient-rich upwelling along the Pacific coast of South America.
Forecasters are monitoring the development of a potential "Super El Niño" for 2026.
A "Super El Niño" is defined by ocean temperatures warming more than 2°C (3.6°F) above average.
Peak impacts of a "Super El Niño" usually occur between December and January.
